definition: Somnolent means drifting toward sleep, eyelids growing heavy.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word somnolent. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know somnolent should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The warm milk and the third bedtime story left Zoe somnolent at last, her questions arriving slower and slower.
Sleepy is the first, mildest tug toward bed—a sleepy child still negotiates for one more story, while somnolent means the slide toward sleep has truly begun.
Comatose goes far beyond sleepy or somnolent—it means unconscious outright, past being roused at all, while somnolent still hovers on sleep's doorstep.

Drowsy is the everyday word for the drift toward sleep—what you say in pajamas. Somnolent is the identical state in formal dress: a writer picks somnolent when the slide toward sleep should be felt in the prose. The difference is register, not meaning.

Soporific describes whatever causes the sleepiness, not the person feeling it: a soporific lecture, the soporific drone of rain. The listener it works on becomes somnolent. If the word answers 'what put you under?', it is soporific; if it answers 'how did you feel?', it is somnolent.
fully awake and tracking everything
unable or unwilling to drift off
Flip the root with in- ('without') and you get insomnia - the complaint that filled her diary all through exam season.

The hammock, the cicadas, and the after-lunch sun made Theo somnolent within minutes; the paperback slid to the grass with his thumb still marking the page.
Somnolent is the precise word for the slide toward sleep—heavier than 'tired,' gentler than 'asleep.' Tired bodies ache; somnolent ones drift, eyelids losing the argument a little at a time.
Somnolent is the dressed-up word for drifting toward sleep—use it when you want that slide to be felt in the prose.
Its unit-mates languid (weak and slow) and torpid (shut down, dormant) describe low energy without the pull toward sleep; somnolent is specifically the closing eyelid.
For plain speech, drowsy does the same work in pajamas.

The glasshouse tour begins briskly enough, docents naming orchids while visitors scribble in the little free notebooks.
But the conservatory is kept at jungle warmth, the air heavy with mist and the smell of wet earth.
By the second wing, the group has gone somnolent: questions trail off, benches fill, and one photographer stops mid-caption.
Docents accept it cheerfully and build in a shaded pause by the koi pool, where nobody pretends to take notes anymore.
Veterans of the tour say the trick is a cold drink beforehand and a hat, and even then the warm fog wins by four o'clock.
